strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 10 MetaWorld manipulation tasks with 8 seeds, including multiple categories of baselines (progress-based reward learning, imitation-from-observation, and privileged methods), providing a fairly rigorous comparison landscape.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of each design choice (implicit negative sampling, exponentially weighted pair sampling, two-hot discretization) as well as comparisons to alternative temporal modeling schemes (only-from-init, single-frame input, order prediction), which convincingly support the specific architectural choices.

The qualitative reward-curve visualizations (Fig. 4) comparing successful vs. failed rollouts provide compelling, interpretable evidence that TimeRewarder better distinguishes productive from unproductive behavior than VIP, PROGRESSOR, and Rank2Reward.

The cross-domain experiment leveraging human videos with only one in-domain demonstration is a nice demonstration of the method's potential scalability to passive, action-free, cross-embodiment video sources.

The paper is clearly written, provides a simple and reproducible method with detailed hyperparameters in the appendix, and a lightweight theoretical motivation connecting temporal distance to potential-based reward shaping.
The method eliminates the need for online reward-model updates (unlike Rank2Reward/PROGRESSOR), which is a practically useful property for scaling to larger passive video datasets.
weaknesses: All quantitative RL results are confined to simulated MetaWorld tasks; even the 'cross-domain' human-video experiment ultimately trains and evaluates the downstream RL policy in the MetaWorld simulator rather than on a real robot, so claims about scalability to 'diverse video sources' and real-world applicability remain only partially substantiated.

The headline claim that TimeRewarder even surpasses the manually engineered environment dense reward on 9/10 tasks is a strong claim that warrants more scrutiny/discussion (e.g., is MetaWorld's dense reward itself suboptimal for these particular tasks, is the DrQ-v2 hyperparameter tuning equally favorable to both settings); the paper does not investigate why or provide additional environments/reward functions to confirm generality of this result.

The theoretical justification (Sec 4.3) relies on strong simplifying assumptions (uniform per-step cost, expert optimality, monotonic progress) that do not hold for demonstrations with pauses, corrections, or non-monotonic progress; the paper's own conclusion acknowledges this as an open limitation but the theory section does not clearly delineate its scope of validity.

The core technical idea (predicting normalized temporal distance/order between frame pairs) is closely related to existing progress-based methods (TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR); the main novelty lies in specific implementation choices (implicit negative via signed distance, weighted sampling, two-hot discretization) rather than a fundamentally new formulation, making the originality contribution moderate/incremental.

The cross-domain human-video experiments are limited in scale (only 3 tasks, 20 videos each) and the improvement from combining human + single MetaWorld video, while notable, still falls short of the 100-demo in-domain baseline, so the practical benefit of leveraging in-the-wild video is only partially demonstrated.

Baseline fairness details (e.g., hyperparameter tuning effort for GAIfO, OT, ADS, PROGRESSOR, Rank2Reward) are not fully specified, leaving some uncertainty about whether baselines were tuned to a comparable degree as the proposed method.
No failure-case or robustness analysis is provided for the real-robot/embodiment-gap setting beyond the 3 selected tasks, limiting insight into when and why the cross-domain transfer might fail.

strengths: The paper is clearly organized and the core idea (learning frame-wise temporal distances as progress-based rewards) is simply stated and easy to follow.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical study on 10 MetaWorld tasks with 8 baselines spanning three categories (progress-based reward learning, ILfO, and privileged methods), plus VOC-metric analysis, qualitative reward-curve visualizations, and an ablation of each design component (implicit negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, two-hot discretization) as well as alternative temporal-modeling variants.
The cross-domain experiment combining a single in-domain MetaWorld demo with real human videos is an interesting proof-of-concept for leveraging heterogeneous passive video sources.
The method is lightweight: once trained, the reward model is frozen during RL, avoiding costly online reward updates that afflict several baselines (e.g., GAIfO, OT/ADS, VIP-style methods).
weaknesses: The headline claim that TimeRewarder surpasses the hand-engineered MetaWorld environment dense reward on 9/10 tasks is extraordinary and under-scrutinized. No investigation is offered into why a purely video-derived proxy would systematically beat a reward explicitly designed with privileged simulator state; possible confounders (reward scaling/weighting differences via the constant α, difference in RL hyperparameter tuning for the two reward types, or degenerate behavior of the environment reward under the modified wide initialization protocol described in A.4.2) are not examined, making the result hard to trust at face value.

The 'theoretical justification' in Sec. 4.3 is largely tautological: it assumes expert optimality, a uniform per-step cost of 1/(T-1), and γ→1, which essentially restates the temporal-distance construction as ground truth rather than providing an independent guarantee that this potential aligns with true task progress under distribution shift (the regime the method is actually deployed in during RL exploration).

Evaluation is confined to short-horizon (200k-step), simulated MetaWorld manipulation tasks; the 'cross-domain' experiment still trains and evaluates policies purely in simulation (human videos are only used for reward pretraining), so claims about scalability to 'diverse video sources' and real-world deployment remain unsubstantiated.

Baselines that explicitly rely on online refinement for stability (Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, per the related-work discussion) appear to be evaluated only in their offline/frozen configuration, which may unfairly handicap them relative to TimeRewarder and undermines the fairness of the comparison the paper's central claims rest on.

Only 8 seeds are used and no statistical significance testing is reported, while several plots (Fig. 5, Fig. 6) show large overlapping variance bands between methods, making some of the claimed 'wins' potentially not robust.

Demonstration/data scale used to validate the 'scalable to large diverse datasets' claim is modest (100 demos per task, 20 human videos per task); no experiment actually stress-tests scaling behavior, so this motivating claim is speculative rather than demonstrated.

The paper acknowledges failure on tasks with back-and-forth motion but does not quantify or analyze this limitation empirically (e.g., which of the 10 tasks failed and why), leaving the stated limitation largely unsubstantiated beyond a brief remark in the conclusion.

Some experimental design choices (e.g., the deliberately widened initialization range in A.4.2, chosen partly because it makes OT/ADS look worse) are introduced without ablating the standard/narrow initialization setting, raising concern that the benchmark protocol may have been tuned in ways that favor the proposed method over trajectory-matching baselines.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly presented: modeling frame-wise temporal distance (rather than pairwise ordering or triple-based relative position) yields a fine-grained, antisymmetric progress signal that can be frozen and used directly as a dense reward without online refinement, unlike several prior progress-based baselines (Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR).

The experimental evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a reward-learning paper: 10 MetaWorld tasks, 8 baselines spanning three method families (progress-based, imitation-from-observation, privileged), a VOC-based generalization probe, qualitative reward-curve visualizations on success/failure rollouts, and a 3-part ablation (implicit negative sampling, weighted sampling, discretization) plus 3 alternative design comparisons.

The theoretical justification (Section 4.3) connects the temporal-distance objective to potential-based reward shaping under a plausible expert-optimality assumption, giving the method some principled grounding rather than being purely heuristic.

The cross-domain experiment leveraging 20 unlabeled real human videos alongside a single in-domain demo is a nice demonstration of scalability toward diverse, action-free video sources, which is central to the paper's motivating claim about scalability.

Reasonable reproducibility: hyperparameters for both the reward model and the RL algorithm are reported in the appendix, and demonstration collection protocol (broadened initialization) is explained with justification for why it affects baseline comparisons (e.g., OT/ADS).
weaknesses: The headline claim that TimeRewarder surpasses the manually engineered environment dense reward on 9/10 tasks is a strong claim that is not sufficiently interrogated; MetaWorld's built-in dense rewards are known in the literature to be imperfectly shaped for some tasks, so this result may partly reflect weaknesses of the baseline dense reward rather than clear superiority of the learned reward. More discussion or an additional stronger dense-reward baseline would strengthen this claim.

All quantitative RL results are confined to MetaWorld simulation; the real-world human video experiments (Q4) only feed into reward learning while downstream policy execution and evaluation still occur in simulation, so claims about applicability to "real-world robotic scenarios" and passive in-the-wild video are not fully validated by a real robot deployment.

Some baselines (VIP, PROGRESSOR, Rank2Reward) are explicitly noted in related work to require online refinement in their original formulations, yet in this paper's comparison they appear to be used in a frozen, expert-only-trained setting; this could understate their achievable performance and make the comparison less than fully fair, even though the frozen-reward property is touted as an advantage of TimeRewarder.

The paper acknowledges a real limitation (tasks with frequent back-and-forth motions) but does not empirically demonstrate on any such task how badly the method degrades, leaving the scope of applicability only partially characterized; task diversity is also limited to short-horizon, single-stage manipulation skills.

No statistical significance testing is reported despite the strong comparative claims across many tasks/baselines; given the visibly large variance bands in Figures 5, 6, 11, and 12, some reported "wins" over baselines or over environment reward may not be robust.

The human video cross-domain results are demonstrated on only 3 tasks with 20 videos each, which is a fairly narrow empirical basis for the broader claim that the method "can exploit real-world human videos" as a generally scalable path to reward learning from diverse video sources.

strengths: The core idea—training a self-supervised model on signed frame-wise temporal distances with implicit negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, and two-hot discretization—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly distinguished from prior progress-based reward learning methods (VIP, GVL, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR).

Extensive experimental evaluation across 10 Meta-World tasks against 8 baselines spanning three categories (action recovery/BC, inverse RL/OT variants, progress-based methods), plus additional comparisons in the appendix (TemporalOT, ORCA, ResNet-34 VIP, from-scratch backbones, ManiSkill3 task), suggesting the results are not cherry-picked to a narrow baseline set.

Multiple complementary analyses beyond aggregate success rate: Value-Order Correlation on held-out trajectories, qualitative reward/value curves on success vs. failure rollouts, and PCA visualization of learned representations, which together build a convincing narrative for why the method works.

A useful theoretical note identifying and proving that VIP's training objective is unbounded/degenerate under a particular (but plausible) implementation detail, which is a nontrivial and potentially impactful observation for the community.

Thoughtful ablations isolating the contribution of each design choice (negative sampling, weighted sampling, discretization) and of alternative formulations (single-frame input, order prediction, progress-from-init), with results that are largely consistent with the paper's narrative.

Cross-domain experiments incorporating real human video demonstrations show a meaningful proof-of-concept that action-free heterogeneous videos can be combined with limited in-domain demonstrations, which is relevant to the paper's scalability claims.

The limitations of the theoretical framework (visual aliasing due to POMDP structure, back-and-forth motion) are explicitly acknowledged and discussed with a proposed (though untested) mitigation via history-conditioning, showing honest treatment of assumptions.
Reasonably detailed hyperparameters and implementation description support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that TimeRewarder even outperforms Meta-World's manually engineered dense reward is a strong, somewhat surprising result; the explanation given (pre-contact progress not captured by hand-crafted reward) is plausible but is asserted rather than rigorously verified, and could reflect idiosyncrasies of Meta-World's specific reward functions rather than a general property.

All primary quantitative results are confined to a single benchmark family (Meta-World) with short-horizon, single-stage manipulation tasks; the one additional ManiSkill3 task is relegated to the appendix and only covers a single simple task (PushCube), leaving generalization to longer-horizon or more complex/multi-stage tasks largely untested.

The real-world/cross-domain experiments are limited in scale (only 3 tasks, 20 human videos each) and the reported gains, while directionally interesting, are based on small sample sizes without strong statistical characterization of significance beyond seed variance bands.

The core theoretical justification (Section 4.3) assumes a fully observable MDP where states are recoverable from single-frame observations; the paper's own example shows this breaks down under visual aliasing/back-and-forth motion, and while acknowledged, no experiment actually tests or resolves this failure mode (e.g., via the proposed history-conditioning extension), leaving a gap between theory and validated practice.

The reward-combination weight α, while shown to be relatively insensitive within the tested range, is still an additional hyperparameter requiring a heuristic (10x max dense reward) that partially contradicts the paper's motivation of removing manual tuning from reward design, and the sensitivity analysis is limited to only 3 tasks.

Novelty is more incremental than transformative: the fundamental idea of exploiting temporal ordering/distance for progress-based rewards is well established in prior work (TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR); the contribution here is largely a combination of known techniques (signed/antisymmetric distance regression, weighted sampling, two-hot discretization) rather than a conceptually new mechanism.

The five-question experimental structure in Section 5.2, while informative, is largely qualitative/illustrative (e.g., single trajectory case studies in Figure 4) rather than statistically rigorous, which somewhat weakens the strength of causal claims about why TimeRewarder outperforms baselines.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental design covering 10 Meta-World manipulation tasks, multiple baseline categories (action recovery, inverse RL/trajectory matching, progress-based methods, privileged methods), and thorough ablations of every proposed component (implicit negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, two-hot discretization).

Identification of a genuine flaw in VIP's training objective (unboundedness, Appendix A.3) is a useful technical contribution that could inform future work using similar implicit time-contrastive objectives.

Several complementary analyses (Value-Order Correlation, PCA visualization of learned representations, qualitative reward curves on success/fail trajectories) provide converging evidence that the learned rewards are temporally coherent and generalize somewhat beyond the training demonstrations.
The cross-domain experiment combining a single in-domain demo with real human videos is a nice illustration of the method's flexibility with heterogeneous, action-free video sources.

Extensive appendix material (alternative backbones, additional simulator ManiSkill3, bin-count ablation, alpha sensitivity, additional OT baselines) suggests the authors made an effort toward robustness checks.
weaknesses: Core technical novelty is incremental: the underlying idea of exploiting temporal ordering/distance as reward is well established (TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, GVL), and TimeRewarder largely combines existing ingredients (bidirectional/signed temporal distance, weighted local sampling, two-hot discretization borrowed from EfficientZero) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism.

The headline claim that the learned proxy reward outperforms the manually engineered environment dense reward on 9/10 tasks is a strong claim that is only partially substantiated — the explanation offered (Meta-World's dense reward is weak in the pre-contact phase) is task/benchmark-specific and undermines the generality of the claim; no comparison on a benchmark with a genuinely strong dense reward is provided.

All quantitative RL results are confined to simulated Meta-World (plus a single added ManiSkill3 task); the 'real-world human video' experiments (Fig. 7) still train and evaluate the downstream policy purely in simulation, with human video only contributing to reward-model training — this significantly tempers the 'exploits real-world human videos' framing suggested in the abstract/intro, since no real robot deployment or evaluation is shown.

The reward-scale balancing coefficient α is tuned adaptively per-method; while an ablation shows TimeRewarder's own sensitivity is low, it is unclear whether the same careful/adaptive tuning was applied equally and fairly to all eight baselines, raising concerns about comparison fairness.

The initialization protocol for Meta-World demonstrations was deliberately widened specifically to break appearance-matching shortcuts exploited by OT-based baselines; while justified as more realistic, this choice was not validated against the baselines' original evaluation protocols, and it specifically advantages the temporal-distance-based proposed method, raising a benchmark-design fairness concern.

The theoretical justification (Section 4.3) is somewhat hand-wavy: it derives a clean equivalence between value function and time-to-go for a fully-observed MDP, but immediately acknowledges this breaks down under partial observability/visual aliasing, and the proposed fix (history-conditioned inputs) is neither implemented nor empirically tested in the main results, leaving the theory largely disconnected from the actual deployed model.

Figures for RL success-rate curves show wide variance bands for many methods and lack explicit statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess whether differences between TimeRewarder and the strongest baselines (e.g., Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR) are reliably significant on tasks where curves visually overlap.
No wall-clock/computational cost comparison is reported despite scalability being a central motivating claim of the paper.

strengths: The core method is simple and well-motivated: learning signed, bidirectional (forward/backward) temporal distance regression naturally yields both a progress signal and an implicit measure of suboptimality, avoiding the need for goal conditioning required by prior work such as VIP and PROGRESSOR.

Experimental evaluation is unusually thorough for a paper of this size: 10 Meta-World tasks, 8 baselines spanning three method families (action recovery/BC, adversarial/OT imitation, and progress-based reward learning), and a large appendix with additional ablations (VIP backbone choice, training from scratch, additional OT-based baselines TemporalOT/ORCA, an additional ManiSkill3 task, sensitivity to the reward-combination weight α and bin count K).

The ablation studies (implicit negative sampling, weighted pair sampling, two-hot discretization) are individually motivated and empirically validated, and the paper goes further to test whether simply adding negative sampling to a baseline (PROGRESSOR) can close the gap, providing a more convincing isolation of the method's benefits than most ablation sections.

The theoretical justification connecting time-to-go value functions to temporal distance is a nice, mostly self-contained derivation, and the paper is commendably honest about where this analysis breaks down in practice (visual aliasing/back-and-forth motions in POMDPs), rather than overclaiming generality.

The appendix identifies and proves a genuine inconsistency between the VIP paper's stated objective and its released code/pseudococde (Appendix A.3), which is a useful and verifiable contribution beyond the main method.

The cross-domain experiment leveraging real human videos alongside a single in-domain demonstration is a compelling proof-of-concept for the paper's scalability narrative, and qualitative analyses (VOC metric, reward curves on success/failure rollouts, PCA of learned representations) provide convincing mechanistic evidence for why the method works, not just aggregate success rates.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the central idea (temporal distance/progress as reward from passive video) is already well established by TCN, VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, and GVL; TimeRewarder's contribution is largely a recombination of existing techniques (signed distance regression, two-hot discretization from EfficientZero, a 1/Δ sampling heuristic) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The claim that TimeRewarder "outperforms even the manually designed environment dense reward" is a striking claim that may say more about Meta-World's specific dense-reward shaping (acknowledged to underweight pre-contact progress) than about a general advantage of learned progress rewards; the claim's generality beyond this benchmark is untested.

Benchmarking is fairly narrow: the main results are entirely on Meta-World (with only a single supplementary ManiSkill3 task and no other RL backbone besides DrQ-v2), and Meta-World success rates for many methods approach ceiling, potentially limiting the benchmark's power to discriminate reward quality.

Real-world validation is limited to reward-learning demonstrations only (3 tasks, cross-domain reward transfer) — there is no full real-robot RL deployment, so claims about the practical scalability of the approach to genuinely in-the-wild video remain partially speculative.

The paper repeatedly emphasizes "9/10 tasks" as the headline result but does not clearly discuss or analyze the one task where TimeRewarder does not win, leaving an evaluative gap in understanding failure modes.

The weighted pair sampling scheme (P(Δ)∝1/Δ) is justified mainly empirically via ablation rather than through principled derivation, and its interaction with the discretization scheme is not deeply analyzed.

The theoretical justification, while honest about limitations, relies on strong simplifying assumptions (deterministic transitions, fully observable state, per-step constant penalty reward) that are quite far from the realistic manipulation settings studied, limiting how much explanatory weight the theory can bear.
